While this game is kinda cute, it's also really bad, with plenty of bad design choices.

- The gameplay is okay-ish during the first few hours, then gets annoyingly repetitive. 
- The dungeons are meh and the fighting system is quite bad, the same monsters are everywhere and the boss fights are tedious.
- The 'main' quest of the game is just ... give money to a NPC, once, twice, once again, and yet another time. Every single side quest is a glorified 'fetch' with bland, boring text. Also some NPC will give you a quest and then disappear for a few days, leaving you unable to turn it in
- Some important shop NPC just ... disappear for entire days ? Little blacksmith lady, I have a full inventory of gear that I need to sell ??
- The upgrade system is terrible, NPCs will simply take away your item (and only one item) for an entire day and you'll only get it back the next day. Alright but I have four items to upgrade several times ... ??
- There's nothing close to a sense of progression in the entire game. The repetitive restaurant keeping never gets upgraded for the entire experience. You could maybe automate things or hire staff (which Dave the Diver did right !) but nah. It's the same thing all along. The advanced dungeons give you the exact same gear as the day one dungeon.

Let me start by saying that it is not a terrible game. However, especially at the asking price of €24.99, there is no way I can recommend it.

So, what’s wrong with it? The game is extremely repetitive and lacks depth. What you see in the first hour is what you get for the next 20–30 hours.

The cooking part is extremely simple. People come in, order things based on what you can make with the ingredients you have, and once they pick a dish, all you have to do is press one button to cook it (and occasionally deliver it to the table for certain customers), then take their money once they are done. That’s it. There is zero difficulty at all, and it’s extremely boring just waiting around and occasionally pressing a button here and there.

As for the dungeons, there are four different ones with randomly generated maps, which partially share enemies with each other (said enemies drop ingredients for the cooking part), making you wonder what the point is of having 4. At least each comes with its own unique mini-bosses on floor 3 and bosses on floor 6 (floor 6 being the last floor of each dungeon). There’s a small variety of weapons and armor, but even when upgrading them, it feels like they don’t do nearly enough damage.

The art style is nice, however, and it does have a decent amount of side quests to do.

Works without any issues on Linux with Proton (9.0-4).

The bones of a good game are here but the balancing, quality of life and progression mechanics are just... missing. Almost like the developers were told to ship, ready or not, and never came back to tweak the small things that would make this game fun.

Example: Every single "quest" is to turn in a stack of resources, and get a new recipe in return. You need the actual resources in your inventory (can't pull from your home storage). So - to turn in the quest, you need to talk to the quest giver, go to your restaurant (after a 10 second loading screen), go to your room (after another 10 second loading screen), grab the resources, go back through the restaurant (10 second loading screen), and then turn in the quest. This unlocks another quest... where you need to do the whole thing again.

Actually running the restaurant is also a slog. It's the only way to make money, but you will acquire resources and ingredients far faster than you could ever actual sell them in the restaurant. Even as you unlock higher-tier recipes that use multiple ingredients at once, the majority of your customers will still order a single boiled egg, meaning you make a whole $14 per ticket. You'll have 500 eggs sitting in your inventory and go through maybe 30 over the course of the 10-minute restaurant phase. At times I was literally watching Netflix while 'running' the restaurant.

This was a hard one to rate, but ultimately, I wouldn't recommend this to anyone unless it's on sale AND you have a lot of spare time on your hands.

The game starts off very simple with a good introduction and feel for your progression, but spirals instantly into what seems like endless fetch quests and bland dialogue from NPC's. The gameplay loop is to run your restaurant with food you cook using ingredients you scavenged. There's nothing else. The dungeons you run through are the exact same layouts with the same annoying enemies unless you cheese them to oblivion.

If you like simple games, then this would be up your alley, but honestly? You probably have better games in your backlog.

The game is very cute and aesthetically pleasing; I like the overall vibe of the game. Although having said that, there are several issues with the game where it's difficult to recommend it.

The restaurant and cooking part of the game: It's very barebones and repetitive. The main draw of the game is the casual cooking theme yet it lacks any sort of depth and variety to keep it engaging. All you do is go to the respective cooking station and press a button to cook the ordered dish immediately and most customers will automatically just walk to the counter to pick up their food then back to their table; there is no need for any user input aside from some particular group of customers. This gameplay loop stays the same throughout the entire game.
It feels like a missed opportunity, as adding mini-games to assess the quality of the food, or introducing customers with unique tastes or preferences, could have added depth and kept things engaging.

On the rogue-like combat side, which is the second main gameplay loop for gathering ingredients, things aren't much better. Enemies are frustratingly tanky, making ingredient grind feel like a slog. This makes the grind feel even more tedious with how little items can stack; You will find yourself constantly running out of backpack space and needing to decide between keeping ingredients or clearing out space for building materials.

Despite these flaws, the game still holds its charm with its cute art, relaxing soundtrack, and overall vib

A very cute game with huge amounts of grinding. You are a restaurant owner and you need to procure your own ingredients from dungeons next to your city. But you also need to run your restaurant!
Thankfully you have magic invisible chefs, but you do not have the same for the cashier. 
A hungry person comes, chooses something from the menu and you run to create it . Once you click what the person wants, then it is being cooked by itself and usually the person who ordered goes to take his food from the counter by himself. There are some customers that you need to serve yourself.

The cashier is being operated by you. So you run to the kitchen, you click what to cook, then go to place where you can see the whole restaurant. If someone wants to pay, you need to collect the money. Not a difficult procedure, but a QoL update could be either a chef or a cashier or the ability to hire staff for your restaurant.

If we go back to the ingredients, you need to grind a lot so you can sell meals, but also to upgrade your items and preparation booths (spots?). A - LOT!

While the game from difficulty wise is ok, it ramps up very fast when you start the quest after the debt.

I would say you can play it, but it may leave a weird aftertaste. I could not suggest it full price. It needs some QoL updates.

I was really excited to try this game with its mix of rogue-like aspects, and restaurant managing reminiscent of Diner Dash. Unfortunately, this game falls extremely short of my expectations, especially for a $24.99 price tag. I feel like there are many other rogue-likes for the same price or cheaper that do the genre far more justice. 

My first main complaint with this game is its lack of visual clarity. Solid green enemies on a solid green background, further invisible under loot you can’t pick up. Certain weapons and effects are opaque to the point you cannot see anything - enemies, traps, the ground, yourself, nothing. Additionally, there is little to no clarity between AoE affects cast by enemies or by yourself when using the same element. There also seems to be inconsistency with terrain collision for enemies versus weaponry versus your character. All in all, I found myself frequently asking “what even hit me???”

My secondary large complaint is a lack of clear progression. Certainly, there are fetch quests to earn recipes and shop upgrades and reputation; but the majority of your game time is in the dungeon, and there is no character upgrades to make yourself stronger. Weapons are upgradable, but the brewing system is unintuitive and barely explained, and standard upgrades take large amounts of resources and time for a minimal and unnoticeable damage increase. Just shy of a reccommend. I love just about every aspect of this game but the combat so clunky. Which is NOT what you want with a game that makes you grind.

Cool concept. The restaurant part is a very chill, simple, but still engaging gameplay loop.
However, the combat part doesn't feel good.
There are very few builds possible, and that’s okay—not every combat system needs to be deep and complex.
The real issue for me is that every combination of equipment feels exactly the same from level one to max level. There is absolutely no sense of progression, and the combat feels slow and clunky from start to finish. In my opinion, it's not worth the time and the grind.
By the way, the game lacks optimization (sometimes NPCs don't appear on screen, for example) and some Quality of Life (QoL) features, like being able to end the day from anywhere or turning in quest items directly from chests.

TLDR: 5/10 A cute game where you serve food. The gameplay loop gets repetitive quickly. (As in not discovering anything new) w/ combat mixed in. (This is NOT a roguelike in any shape or form)  
 
What I like: Anime art style. Nothing to write home about though. Serving customers quickly/efficiently. The boss battles (a little)(The combat is basically two attack buttons and a dodge w/ some slots used for healing) The first boss you come across is a [spoiler] chicken. It has a lot more than two move sets which surprised me. [/spoiler] Considering the games theme.  
 
What I disliked: Literally can't move the camera... It's fixed to one angle. "Action Roguelike" Yeah not really. The environment changes yeah, do the abilities or enemies change? No. So there literally is nothing "Roguelike" about it. It's about the same as calling default Minecraft a "Action Roguelike"... The gameplay loop gets boring really quickly. Go into a dungeon to farm ingredients to use for your restaurant. Get money to upgrade your restaurant/gear/do a quest here and there. The real boring part is seeing pretty much the same environment/enemies the while 14+ hours I've played. I wanted to increase the foot traffic my restaurant got but had no real idea how to do that. I added more seats than I really needed. I added specific furniture to increase certain visitors (those furniture never said it would increase the over all foot traffic. Just a higher chance those customers would show up)

I love games like Touhou Mystia's Izakaya, dave the diver, moonlighter where you go dungeon at day and manage a restaurant at night. But... in order for these games to be good... you need a good dungeon. that could be done by having a good battle mechanism, good exploration/map design, etc. This game is... meh. The devs clearly did not have any understanding of what made these kinda games fun. 
mystia's izakaya didn't have a dungeon, but that was a little different. It was more of a story based game with affection system to make up for the lack of a dungeon, and each characters had their unique charm. (I mean, it's touhou so...)

but this game was very meh.
in a dungeon, there really isn't any level design.
you only have two attacks. mouse left click and a long ranged attack with a cooldown.

Disappointing... :( The combat in the dungeon crawling part of the game has clunky controls and the cooking part of the game, which I was looking forward to most, is very lackluster. It's a shame because the concept is amazing and the art is fantastic! Sad that the gameplay is lacking...

Could a person enjoy this game?  Absolutely... and I don't mean that in a "there's always someone that enjoys something" kind of way, I mean it is fair to think most will enjoy this game, but for me, the game gets in its own way in a variety of ways that, by themselves are not too bad but, put together it literally made me uninstall the game twice with months apart before I installed again.

I really dislike heavy RNG, especially when there's no rhyme or reason to it.  There's an upgrade system but you can only upgrade 1 trait (you get locked out from ever upgrading the other) and upgrading ALSO possesses RNG.

Lately I've been about 100%ing more of my games rather than buying new ones so it is likely I will endure the slog to do that with this game, but I don't find this game fun...

But if you don't care about a game failing to hide how repetitive it is, is lacking immensely in actual progression, having everything be entirely random regardless as to how far you are in the game, and you just want passable combat with a cute environment and not so bad music... this might be fun for you.

+++ Interesting and novel relationship between dungeon-crawling and cooking. 
+++ Cutesy character design and artwork. 
 
--- Utterly, offensively tone-deaf storyline. 
--- Tediously over-extended game sections. 
--- Uneven difficulty spikes, especially around bosses. 
--- Shallow and unsatisfying upgrade system. 
--- Poorly optimised, with heavy particle effects causing significant slowdowns. 
 
Like an abusive relationship, this title performs the despicable feat of putting the player down while playing it off as harmless comedy. Perhaps this could've worked with a softer touch, but as things stand now, the player character is essentially a non-person who gets bossed around by everyone they encounter, and this vibe unfortunately kills most if not all enjoyment that can be had. The gameplay feels like work being imposed on the player, with sequences that have a tendency to overstay their welcome, and goalposts that feel like they get moved back with every milestone of progress. The backhanded comments and the thinly veiled insults never once relent, lasting all the way to the very end, and it's the kind of toxic environment that makes one want to hit retirement as soon as possible. And here, retirement quite simply comes in the form of a red X.

Cuisineer feels completely hollow and unfinished. 

NPCs have nothing to say to you unless a fetch quest is involved. The only real interaction you have with NPCs for that matter, [i]is[/i] fetch quests. There's a flimsy narrative about paying off your parents' debt, but it doesn't even meet the barren standards of the game it's primarily aping, Recettear. It's introduced quickly and immediately forgotten, with an NPC simply standing around in town who you can pay off, one debt tier at a time, to unlock each successive dungeon.

The dungeons themselves are standard action RPG fare, consisting of arenas connected by doors, feeling a bit like the dungeons in Bastion albeit with none of the creativity or challenge (rather than Hades, what a callback). You'll spend most of the game there, beating up too-small enemies with bloated health values, unreliable hitstun, and outrageous damage values, as well as rocks and trees to farm materials for furniture and expanding the restaurant, because of course you need to grind for materials, too, and not just ingredients.

The experience is mind-numbing, particularly because of the sheer breadth of the dungeons, the sponginess of the enemies, and the sheer amount of any given item you'll need from day to day. It's only made worse by a double whammy of limited inventory space and small stack sizes. There's not even really any sense of risk imposed by any of this, either, as you can teleport out of the dungeon at any time, no matter where you

The idea is fun, but unfortunately, the execution fails at each and every step. And I don't mean just the overall grindy nature of the game, but rather specific issues, which could have been easily made right. 
 
A (not quite) few examples: 
 
1) Inventory management. Maxed out inventory is 40 items. And that includes both ingredient/resource stacks (up to 30) AND single inventory items (gear drops). Going through a dungeon fills you up with 4 types of resources (which you generally need in hundreds each) and at least 12 of the 20 ingredients in existence, which you can do with a single stack each easily, except... See point 3... But there are also unstackable gear drops you might wanna haul home to sell, or use, or whatever... Which wouldn't have been a problem, except... See points 2, 4 and 5. Setting the stack size to 100 would have mitigated most of this artificial anality. 
 
2) You cannot drop some item. You can only discard it permanently. So you've got your inventory full, you can't pick up new items instead of something in your inventory to compare unless you DESTROY something first. It's ok if you wanna pick up ingredients (except... See point 3), but you can't check the dropped gear unless you pick it up first.

Really wanted to like this but every aspect of the game is underdeveloped. There is no meaningful storyline or development of the town, improvements to your restaurant don't have any real effect beyond aesthetics, combat is also extremely simplistic with only a few weapon and upgrade types.

It's very cute- but it just feels, how to put it- uncomfortable to play?
 
I got very confused about what I was actually supposed to be doing multiple times. Instructions coming in the mail is cute- but they're not paced well. I had multiple Dine and Dashers before I ever got the memo on it, and I got a notification about expansion before I'd even bought a second set of tables and chairs. Interacting with characters was also under explained- It was a character's birthday, so I made her a meal as a gift, only to not be able to give it to her. I ended up trashing it, which you do to a lot of items in this game.

The Dungeons are a little too zoomed out and very visually cluttered, half the time I'd think I cleared a room only to take damage and realize I was looking right at a monster and hadn't noticed. Your bag size, even with upgrades, is ridiculously small considering a dungeon run takes a whole day and ingredients only stack to 30 and share space with weapons and armor.

I really wanted to like this game. The characters are adorable, the world building is clever, and the idea of dungeon exploring to get ingredients for a restaurant is so charming, but I can't get over how it feels like I'm fighting to play the game instead of fighting the monsters.
Very cute but lacks depth and mechanics, the gameplay loop is repetitive and gets boring quickly. The art is so adorable, really a pity the townspeople dont have more personality

If you put this game down for multiple months then come back to it for a quick session, you won't feel lost wondering what you're supposed to do then quit feeling annoyed. It super adorable, pretty easy (even for me who's straight up horrible with any video games and if you want a challenge you can up the difficulty) 

The main (and only reason really) i'm not recommending this game is due to it's memory leak issue. i managed to play up to 7-8h before it started to cause massive stutter and became unplayable over time. As long as a patch isn't provided i cannot recommend it sadly.

The game is really cute and the loop is fun enough at first, but it feels like it never progresses into anything that's actually engaging. I got to a point where I was doing dull dungeon runs just to upgrade one bit of my kitchen at a time and the dungeons just aren't fun enough to justify it. When I'm at a point where I'm thinking "I should force myself to finish it", it's probably a bad sign.

Verdict: Honestly, I do not have a whole lot to say about this one. It checked some of the boxes I look for in this type of game, but just wasn't what I was looking for. I am a little particular with regard to what I look for in my cozy-type cooking/farming sims, and this one just didn't do it for me. Not that this is a bad game by any stretch of the imagination--just not my thing.

I love XSEED and Marvelous like Runefactory 3 & 4 were so fun ive been playing their games ever since so this one seemed hopeful.. and while it is cute, I cant recommend it because of the actual game play. Its really repetitive, but also somehow slow? The kitchen experience is not necessarily hectic or exciting (like overcooked! or diner dash or any other cooking/dining sim games), and the dungeons are so repetitive it gets boring after awhile. Any 'collect-a-thon' aspect is already over before the game even starts it feels like... IDK i am just left wanting alot more. Cute game, got boring fast  5/10

This game is unfortunately undercooked. There's no interesting mechanics to any of it. Sometimes it gets busy in the restaurant, and you are too distracted left clicking ovens to realize how boring it is, but there's like nothing to do in this game. No advanced crafting trees, no meaningful decorating, no depth to the combat. It's all just leftclicking till you win. No thought needed, no creativity allowed. My friend made it further in and assures me it doesn't get any better.

First of all, thanks to the devs for not giving up on the game and for releasing a nice little patch!
The first time I tried it, I stopped playing after just 5 hours. But now, the new features actually make me want to jump back in. It's just a shame that it took 2 years to do it.

As for the game itself... I'm really torn.
On one hand, I kinda like it. But on the other, there are so many little things that gradually make me lose the fun a have from this game.
Cuisineer is a GOOD GAME, but it could’ve gone even further with just a bit more effort.
Here’s a list of things that disappointed/annoyed me:

---- No hard mode ----
You’ve got normal, easy, very easy, and casual…
Four difficulty levels designed to make the game less challenging.
In a roguelike, there should be at least some degree of challenge, and players should feel proud of overcoming something that requires reflexes and good judgment.
Here, you can just rush in without caring about your health bar. That’s not my definition of a roguelike.
I understand that some people want to play in chill mode, but three levels for decreasing difficulty and nothing for increase?! That’s a bit much.

---- Restaurant management is way too basic ----
You click on a piece of furniture, the food makes itself, flies onto the counter by itself, and the customers just come grab it—even the nobles!
There’s nothing fun about it.
Most indie games of this type have a cooking system with a bar (black/yellow/green, for example), where you have

I’ve put in over 40 hours into Cuisineer, hoping it would grow on me, but I can confidently say it’s not that great. The restaurant gameplay is extremely limited — it’s basically just clicking to serve what’s requested, with no real choice or creativity in what you make. That aspect gets repetitive fast.

The dungeon crawling, unfortunately, isn’t much better. The damage scaling is way too high, making combat feel almost impossible at times. It’s clunky, unbalanced, and more frustrating than fun.

The story is shallow, and there’s not much to keep you invested long-term. Honestly, the only thing this game has going for it is the cute art style. If you’re looking for a meaningful cooking sim or an engaging action RPG, this isn’t it. I wouldn’t recommend it.

Ah this game is so conflicting. I want to like it so badly, I even found myself pushing through game play I didn't enjoy hoping there were things I just didn't unlock or understand yet, but it is just missing depth. In my mind this game is meant to be 3 different things- a restaurant manager, a dungeon crawler, and a social sim.

As a restaurant manager, the game play is underwhelming. There is no interactivity to the cooking or serving. Either have steps to a recipe or at least require the player to serve the dishes. I spent most of the time in the restaurant waiting for time to pass. It is boring. The dinner and lunch rushes don't raise the stakes at all. There is no risk of ever failing to meet a customer's needs. 

As a dungeon crawler, it is just grinding. Even basic enemies on the first floor of the first dungeon require multiple full combos to kill. All of the enemies just have an insane amount of health (and not in a challenging way). The buff mechanics of the game don't really compensate for this at all. They can increase debuffs applied to the enemies, but at the end of the day you have to sit there and hit attack way too many times for the basic enemies. It doesn't add any challenge, it just slows down the game play to an unenjoyable pace. Even the materials you break require a full combo to destroy and you need basic materials for everything. The NPCs are bland and barely have any dialogue. The town doesn't feel alive at all. The gameplay is grindy and repetitive.

This game is by no means a bad game, but it just feels like the developers wanted to mix all the elements of their favorite games together but didn't add any of the depth. I know this is meant to be a cozy and chill game but the restaurant section really doesn't have any gameplay, it's just click the item the customer wants and sit there. The roguelike section is also too simple, there seems to be a lot of systems but they all ultimately don't affect a run at all. It makes all the runs feel the exact same and that's the last thing you want in a roguelike game.

I'm left a bit disappointed as the premise of the game really sounded like everything I enjoy in games but something about it just never clicked. If it sounds interesting and you're okay with a simple game I would try it for an hour or two, as the gameplay loop doesn't change at all after the first few days. I played for a few more hours but ultimately my feelings about the game didn't change.

This game is *fine* - it's a 6.5/10 game with no major "I Quit" moments.

It's also a Restaurant Management game, with the most basic "Tap Pop-up Bubbles" to complete the Dishes, with no real nuance.
It's a game with Hoard slaying combat, but with very little distracting you from move and tap attack to win.
If you play the first hour, you will know every mechanic this game is going to throw at you.
Even mechanics I'd assumed the game had, ended up being much less consequential when it actually came to use them.

I don't think it's impossible for them to make this into a great game - the best part of this game is the Aesthetics and you can see from those this was crafted with love. But it needs that Unique Selling Point. Either lean into more complex Restaurant mechanics - (Have multistage Food, Have furniture actually increase the "total" number of customers per day, More Functional Objects) - or lean into this being the non-cozy Brawler - (Level ups and Skill Trees, Weapon upgrading being useful, Unique Boss Drops) - but don't leave it as it is; a fairly bland cress sandwich of a game.

I wanted to like this, I really did.

Tedious unfun restaraunt management. There's no skill or method to cooking, you just are clicking a button and waiting over and over again.

Dungeon combat is poorly balanced. You start off with a weapon that does 10 damage and after putting in significant money to upgrade for it to do 11 damage, lol.

Expensive accessories like gloves and boots give you 5HP each.

You can't level up Pom herself, and your inventory is tiny so everything you need to do is frustrating and grindy. 

I can't imagine how anybody would unlock every tea, for example.

There's a solid base here, and with some design improvements, it could be a fun game. However, it's just a waste of potential at the moment, and I can't recommend it.

I wish there was a middle option to leave for a review bc that's what I would give this one. For the price of this game, it is not worth it. Its fine? But there is so little to it that I get bored of it so quickly. It feels like a mobile game honestly. It doesnt feel like there is any progression, and these characters that look SO cool and lovely feel like place holders. You don't get to know them at all, cant do anything for their birthdays, and the only interaction you get from anyone is from side quests that unlocks recipes. There is no challenge on the town side and the only goal you have for the game is to like... grind(its not even a grind, its very easy to get the things you need) for the materials to allow you to upgrade basically just storage space. 

The art and world is VERY cute and lovely, and if you really want something mindless to do then you'll probably like it, but if you're into cozy games for the progression side of it, you won't really find it with this one. Combat is fine, and it feels like you can do some creative things with all the combinations it gives you but even the basic stuff works so it feels pointless to even do that. I'd give it a try if you're interested in it, but once you've gotten like an hour of playtime in, you'll know the game at that point. At the very least, catch it on a sale.

I was drawn in by the nice art style and pretty impressive combat design in the dungeons.  However, actually running the restaurant is extremely dull.  A lot of time is spent waiting for new customers to show up or them to order.  They even collect their own food, so you just queue up whatever they order (through a context menu so you don't even have to remember) and wait until they're ready to pay.  I got no sense of what new mechanics I might look forward to or how to better prepare my restaurant.  One day was marked as "Chicken" day, but I could not actually tell if customers were ordering chicken more often.
